topics.overview: Amino-acid products range from single amino acids to blends. For rehab, whole-protein foods usually cover everyday needs.

claims.statement: Most rehab patients meet amino-acid needs through varied dietary protein rather than isolated amino-acid stacks.
claims.summary: Isolated amino acids have niche research uses; marketing stacks are a poor substitute for progressive loading and total nutrition quality.

topics.overview: For most training and desk days, water and normal meals beat fancy electrolyte tubs. Salts matter more in long hot sessions or medically advised fluid plans.

claims.statement: Everyday MSK recovery rarely requires commercial electrolyte products.
claims.summary: Drink to thirst and habitual needs unless a clinician gave a specific plan. Long hot sessions, heavy sweating, or illness change the picture.

topics.overview: Boswellia extracts appear in some joint-comfort products. Evidence is limited compared with core osteoarthritis care.

claims.statement: Evidence for boswellia in osteoarthritis is limited and not a substitute for NICE-recommended core treatments.
claims.summary: Exercise, education, and supported self-management remain first-line. Discuss herbals with a pharmacist for interactions before self-experimenting.

topics.overview: Calcium is essential for bone health. Food sources are preferred; supplements are considered when diet or medical advice indicates a gap.

claims.statement: Adequate calcium intake supports bone health, ideally from dietary sources first.
claims.summary: NHS nutrient advice and osteoporosis pathways emphasise calcium plus vitamin D context, falls prevention, and strength — not calcium tablets as a stand-alone MSK cure.

topics.overview: Chondroitin is often paired with glucosamine in joint complexes. Expectation management matters more than product price.

claims.statement: Chondroitin has mixed evidence for osteoarthritis symptoms and is not a NICE-recommended core treatment.
claims.summary: As with glucosamine, NG226 focuses on education, exercise, and supported self-management. Supplements are optional adjuncts with uncertain benefit.

topics.overview: Cod liver oil supplies omega-3s plus vitamins A and D. Total vitamin A intake matters — more is not always safer.

claims.statement: Cod liver oil can contribute meaningful vitamin A and D alongside omega-3s; avoid stacking multiple high-A products without advice.
claims.summary: Check combined intakes from multivitamins and cod liver oil. Pregnancy and some medical conditions need individual advice on vitamin A.

topics.overview: Collagen supplements are popular for tendons and joints. Any trial should sit alongside progressive loading — not instead of it.

claims.statement: Tendon and joint capacity are primarily rebuilt with well-timed progressive loading.
claims.summary: MSK rehab evidence consistently prioritises graded exercise for tendinopathy and many osteoarthritis programmes. Collagen powder without that stimulus is unlikely to remodel tissue on its own.

claims.statement: Evidence that collagen supplements improve tendon or joint outcomes is emerging but mixed.
claims.summary: Some small trials explore collagen (sometimes with vitamin C) around training. Products and protocols differ; treat marketing claims cautiously and keep protein intake from food in view.
caveats: People with kidney disease need individualised protein advice.

topics.overview: Devil’s claw is a traditional herbal sometimes marketed for joint or back discomfort. Evidence quality is limited; safety and interactions still matter.

claims.statement: Evidence that devil’s claw meaningfully improves back or joint pain is limited.
claims.summary: Do not delay assessment of red-flag back pain. Prefer guideline-based MSK care and ask a pharmacist before herbal concentrates.

claims.statement: Fish-oil supplements supply long-chain omega-3s; food sources remain the preferred starting point for most people.
claims.summary: See also the omega-3 topic notes. Label EPA/DHA content clearly and avoid rancid products.

topics.overview: Glucosamine is a long-standing joint supplement with inconsistent trial results. Strength, pacing, and weight management (where relevant) change function more reliably.

claims.statement: Evidence that glucosamine improves osteoarthritis pain or structure is inconsistent.
claims.summary: NICE does not recommend glucosamine for osteoarthritis management in NG226. Some people report small comfort changes; others notice nothing. Define a trial period and keep rehab central.
caveats: Shellfish-derived products and anticoagulant therapy need product-specific checks.

topics.overview: ‘Anti-inflammatory’ supplement claims are often broader than the evidence. Distinguish systemic inflammatory disease from everyday MSK tissue irritability.

claims.statement: Most activity-related musculoskeletal pain is managed with load modification and rehab, not anti-inflammatory capsules alone.
claims.summary: Clinical pathways for non-specific back pain, tendinopathy, and osteoarthritis prioritise assessment, movement, and supported self-management. Supplements are optional adjuncts at best.

topics.overview: Insomnia with MSK pain needs careful triage. Sedating herbals are not first-line; persistent insomnia deserves medical pathways.

claims.statement: Cognitive behavioural approaches and sleep hygiene are preferred over unregulated supplement stacks for chronic insomnia.
claims.summary: NICE guidance on insomnia emphasises assessment and non-medicine options first where appropriate. In the UK, melatonin is generally prescription-only for specific uses.
caveats: New snoring, breath pauses, or morning headaches deserve medical review.

claims.statement: Krill oil provides omega-3 fats; claims beyond dose-equivalent EPA/DHA should be treated cautiously.
claims.summary: Shellfish allergy is relevant for some krill products. See omega-3 topic notes for broader framing.

topics.overview: Magnesium is an essential mineral involved in muscle and nerve function. Food sources cover needs for many adults; supplements are most relevant when intake is low or a clinician has identified a gap — not as a stand-alone fix for back spasm.

claims.statement: Magnesium contributes to normal muscle function and is obtained mainly from food.
claims.summary: UK and international nutrient references recognise magnesium’s role in muscle and nervous-system physiology. Leafy greens, nuts, seeds, and whole grains are primary food sources.

claims.statement: Evidence that magnesium supplements reliably prevent idiopathic muscle cramps in the general population is limited.
claims.summary: Cochrane review work on magnesium for cramps has not shown clear benefit for most people with idiopathic cramps. Persistent or severe cramps still deserve medical review; rehab and load management remain central in MSK care.
caveats: Kidney disease and some medicines change magnesium advice — check with a pharmacist or GP.

topics.overview: Long-chain omega-3 fats (EPA/DHA) from oily fish support general health. Concentrated supplements are sometimes discussed for inflammatory joint symptoms, but they do not replace graded loading or medical care.

claims.statement: Eating oily fish regularly is a sensible default for long-chain omega-3 intake.
claims.summary: NHS dietary advice includes oily fish as part of a balanced diet. Food-first approaches avoid many dosing and quality issues of concentrates.

claims.statement: Evidence that omega-3 supplements meaningfully change osteoarthritis or tendon outcomes is mixed and usually modest.
claims.summary: Some inflammatory pathways are biologically plausible targets, but rehab loading, sleep, and activity modification remain the main MSK levers. High doses can affect bleeding risk with anticoagulants.
caveats: Check with a pharmacist before high-dose oils if you bruise easily or take anticoagulants.

claims.statement: Adequate dietary protein supports muscle adaptation when combined with progressive resistance or rehab loading.
claims.summary: Sports nutrition and ageing-muscle literature consistently couple protein intake with training stimulus. Older adults often under-eat protein without noticing.

topics.overview: Stress and pain amplify each other. Sleep, caffeine timing, and load balance usually matter more than a stack of ‘calm’ capsules.

claims.statement: Poor sleep and high stress can increase pain sensitivity and reduce rehab adherence.
claims.summary: Pain science and clinical guidelines for persistent MSK pain emphasise sleep, mood, and activity pacing alongside tissue-focused care.

topics.overview: Curcumin extracts are sometimes tried for joint comfort. Kitchen turmeric is not the same as a high-dose extract; interactions and absorption additives matter.

claims.statement: Curcumin may offer modest symptom relief for some people with osteoarthritis; effects are usually small and not a substitute for exercise-based care.
claims.summary: Reviews of curcumin for knee osteoarthritis report variable, often modest benefits. NICE OA care still centres on information, exercise, weight management where relevant, and appropriate analgesia — not herbals as first-line disease modifiers.
caveats: Piperine-enhanced products can alter medicine metabolism — ask a pharmacist.
Gallbladder disease, surgery plans, and anticoagulants need review before concentrates.

topics.overview: Vitamin C supports normal collagen formation and immune function. Deficiency is uncommon on varied diets in the UK; megadoses are not a tendon shortcut.

claims.statement: Vitamin C contributes to normal collagen formation; food sources are usually sufficient.
claims.summary: NHS nutrient pages describe vitamin C roles and food sources. Pair any collagen discussion with loading rehab rather than relying on a single vitamin.

topics.overview: Vitamin D supports bone and muscle health. UK guidance commonly recommends a maintenance dose through darker months; deficiency treatment belongs under medical supervision with blood results where indicated.

claims.statement: UK public health advice commonly includes considering a daily vitamin D supplement in autumn and winter.
claims.summary: NHS and SACN-linked advice reflects limited winter UV in the UK. Standard maintenance doses differ from high-dose treatment of confirmed deficiency.

claims.statement: Low vitamin D does not explain every episode of back, neck, or joint pain.
claims.summary: Vitamin D status can matter for bone health and some generalised aches, but MSK presentations still need load, sleep, and red-flag assessment. Guessing megadoses from symptoms alone is unsafe.
caveats: Excess vitamin D can raise calcium to unsafe levels.
Some medical conditions need individual advice before supplementing.

claims.statement: Whey protein can help people meet daily protein targets when appetite or time is limited.
claims.summary: Evidence for athletic performance supplements emphasises total daily protein and training quality. Lactose intolerance and kidney disease need individual advice.

topics.overview: Zinc supports normal immune and tissue function. Deficiency is a medical nutrition issue; megadosing is not an MSK shortcut.

claims.statement: Zinc is an essential micronutrient; routine high-dose zinc for musculoskeletal pain lacks strong support.
claims.summary: Meet needs through diet where possible. Long-term high doses can cause copper imbalance and other harms — pharmacist advice matters.
